name: Swim: Full Session
description: Freestyle technique session: kick drills, rotation drills, then swim with one thing to think about. Drills go first while you're fresh. Distances are in LENGTHS (one way). Roughly 1200-1500 total.

dayOverview.theme: Two things, in order: a small, loose kick, then a body that rolls. The kick goes first while your legs are fresh, and it should feel like almost nothing — a big kick burns your air and barely moves you. Then rotation, still the heart of the session: a flat body makes the arms do all the work.

spotlights.why: The kick is what's wearing you out. The wall takes away travel and breathing so you can feel where the kick starts — the hip — before you ask it to move you.

The highest-yield drill for a self-taught swimmer who has never drilled. It forces rotation, forces the legs to work, and teaches breathing off the roll — all with the arms parked so they can't compensate.

watchpoints: Water in the mouth on a breath is a LATE roll, not a small one. Arrive on your side before you ask for air, and keep the lower goggle wet.
🛑 Nothing here is an effort session. Winded at a slow pace means the kick is too big — shrink the kick before anything else.

🛑 The drills run on your legs — every pause on your side, the kick is the only engine. When the kick goes big and ragged, stop drilling and just swim. Drilling past that point grooves the ragged kick.
🛑 Right shoulder: freestyle recovery is a big overhead arc. If it gets crabby, stop the swim, not just the drill.

Count strokes on one full-stroke length near the start, and one on the last length you swim — whenever you decide to stop. Not on drill lengths, where the kick carries you through the pauses. **Your baseline is ~18-20 per length.** It's the only number worth having, and it should drift DOWN over weeks.

exercises.notes: Easy. No thinking, no fixing. Just get wet and let the shoulders open up.

exercises.distance: as far as feels good — around 40 lengths
exercises.notes:
Normal swimming. **One thought only: roll on EVERY stroke, not just the breathing ones.**
- If you arrive at the breath already on your side, the breath is nearly free — the face is almost clear before you ask for air.
- **Lead arm stays long and patient.** On a right-side breath that's the LEFT arm out front. If it presses down early the shoulder drops and the mouth goes under.
- Keep alternating sides — left, right, left. The right side gets easier as the roll improves, not by forcing it.
- **Once the roll feels natural, swap the one thought to: the smallest kick you can get away with.** Knees nearly straight, kick from the hip. If your breathing calms down and your legs don't sink, that's your kick. If they sink, lean harder on your chest before you kick harder.
- **Count strokes on one length** early, and on whatever turns out to be your last one. Same effort, fewer strokes = it's working. Baseline is ~18-20.
- **Stop when it stops feeling good, or when the day needs you.** The distance is not the point — **the drills ran first on purpose, so cutting the main swim short still leaves the session intact.**
Easy backstroke — opens the chest and unloads the front of the shoulder after all that freestyle.

tips: Drills go FIRST, while you're fresh. A drill done tired just grooves the bad version.
Slow is correct on the drills. They are not conditioning — rest at the wall until your breathing settles, however long that takes.
If the throat gums up partway through, ease off for a length and clear it rather than pushing through — outdoor pools and a steady nose-exhale both help.
Breathing on both sides is the right pattern. The weak side is a rotation problem, not a weak-side problem.
Stroke count is the only number worth tracking here. Not laps, not time.
